headline: Nasdaq claws back from correction as dip-buyers stay engaged
body: This week's action was a study in whiplash. Thursday's roughly 4.4% plunge in the S&P 500 was its worst session since April 2025 and pushed the Nasdaq more than 10% below the record it set last month, squarely into correction territory. The proximate trigger was a renewed bout of AI-valuation anxiety — the same data-center-capex worry that has resurfaced repeatedly this year — compounded by post-midterm positioning. Friday brought a partial reversal: a stronger-than-expected jobs report helped the Nasdaq 100 rebound roughly 2% and the S&P 500 edge higher, even as the Dow lagged. For the week overall the Nasdaq still finished down about 3.4% and the S&P 500 off 2.7%, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 4.85%, suggesting the bounce reflected relief more than any real shift in the underlying valuation debate.

Retail behavior has been the more telling signal this year, and the pattern largely held: dip-buying in AI and semiconductor names has stayed a defining feature of 2026, with prior selloffs of comparable size drawing some of the fastest retail inflows in months. The data also show that enthusiasm has been gradually cooling, though — several of the weakest dip-buying responses on record showed up earlier this year, even before this week's drop. Concrete, same-day retail chatter for this specific selloff was thin in what's publicly available, so this read leans more on price action, yields, and the capex narrative than on confirmed social-sentiment specifics. Taken together, the setup looks like a market still conditioned to buy weakness in AI leaders, but doing so with less conviction than earlier in the cycle.
